source.title: Sparsity Moves Computation: How FFN Architecture Reshapes Attention in Small Transformers

record.tranche_reason: Measures grokking timelines on modular addition, an algorithmic task named in the claim, and reports test accuracy reaching 99% during training. It varies architecture and training conditions rather than reproducing the full training-set-size claim.
record.gate_note: The grokking timeline and test-accuracy results are recorded. Component-ablation, Fourier-structure, and histogram-counting results are not rows because they do not measure the grokking behavior named by the tested version. The text does not report a training-set-size sweep or explicitly quantify the gap between training-accuracy saturation and the test-accuracy rise.
record.test_reason: Appendix D trains one-layer Transformers on (a+b) mod 113 with Nanda et al.'s recipe: 30% train split, full batch, AdamW, weight decay 1.0. It reports epoch-to-99% test accuracy and how many seeds grok within 40k epochs, across FFN variants. That bears on whether delayed generalization appears on this algorithmic task (V1). Grokking is a secondary result; the paper's main subject is FFN-to-attention redistribution. The text never gives training-accuracy saturation times and never varies training-set size.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase covers only a secondary appendix. The main conclusion is about redistribution. Sparse top-1 MoE routing moves computation from the FFN to attention in one-layer Transformers, strongest on add-7. This comes from reduced per-token capacity plus sparse partitioning, not learned routing. GLU gating rotates Fourier structure out of the neuron basis. On grokking, the authors report that MoE speeds it up and makes it more reliable on modular addition. Because dropout does better, they call this an optimization-side regularization effect rather than a primary contribution.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modular addition and test-accuracy grokking timelines, but emphasizes FFN architecture and routing comparisons; it does not test the training-set-size relationship in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with FFN architecture, routing type (learned, random, top-2), model width, dropout, and auxiliary-loss coefficient. Random routing is slower and less reliable than learned routing; top-2 does not grok within 40k epochs; the MoE-vs-FFN timing difference grows with width in the reported sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse top-1 MoE routing speeds up grokking and makes it more reliable than a parameter-matched dense FFN. The advantage needs multiple experts (the E=1 control does not speed it up) and grows with width. Dropout 0.3 is faster still.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The timing and reliability of grokking depend on FFN architecture and regularizing sparsity, not only on data size and weight decay.

fits_no_version.finding: GLU gating lowers per-neuron Fourier concentration on modular addition (0.17 vs FFN 0.34) while PCA still recovers Fourier-aligned subspaces. Histogram counting strategies differ by architecture (relation-style vs inventory-style).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The same algorithm can be represented in architecture-dependent bases; learned strategies can differ by FFN architecture.

record.problems: The evidence is from one-layer, small algorithmic models and modular addition. Most timeline experiments use 5 seeds, while the 20-seed comparison is reported for FFN and learned MoE. The study does not report the training-accuracy saturation point or a training-set-size sweep, so it does not establish the full V1 timing and dataset-size pattern.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant grokking outcomes left out. Component-ablation and Fourier measurements were excluded because they measure redistribution or representation rather than the delayed test-generalization behavior in V1.

untested.parts: When training accuracy saturates relative to the test-accuracy jump; whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks (only a 30% split is used); algorithmic tasks other than modular addition.
No time course of Fourier-circuit formation or memorization removal. Fourier concentration is measured only on final checkpoints.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm sweep. Fig. 6b reports weight-norm ratios during grokking but tests no lazy/rich switch.
Weight decay is fixed at 1.0. The weight-decay baseline in Fig. 16 has no reported numbers. No critical dataset size or ungrokking.
No test of whether runs converge to the same algorithm. GLU and FFN Fourier-basis differences are representational and are listed under fits_no_version.
No optimizer-instability or softmax floating-point controls.

missing.what: E=1 control (auxiliary loss, no routing) does not accelerate grokking
SiLU GLU: 1/5 seeds fails to grok on modular addition (final 31.5%); MoE-GLU does not show this
MoE-GLU shows no learned-routing grokking speedup
Weight-decay regularization baseline results (no numbers given in text)
Norm vs no-norm grokking curves (figure only, no numbers)
Final modadd accuracy for dense FFN below 100% (66.8% GELU, 79.7% SiLU 5-seed means), reflecting non-grokking seeds

record.verdict_notes: Grokking evidence is a secondary appendix result. It supports only the existence of delayed generalization in Nanda's setup, without training-accuracy timing or a dataset-size sweep. The text conflicts on the random-routing median: ~33k in Sec. 4.2 vs ~27,500 in App. D.2. Several reader 'partial' states measured the MoE-vs-FFN speedup rather than V1's effect and were corrected.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports grokking on modular addition, but does not explicitly measure when training accuracy saturates relative to test accuracy, or test whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks. The timelines concern modular addition, not multiple algorithmic datasets.
No time-course analysis of circuit formation or memorizing-component removal; Fourier analyses are not reported as continuous progress measures predicting the test-accuracy rise.
No non-algorithmic data or initialization-scale/weight-norm sweep testing delayed generalization.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
The study mentions weight-decay baselines but reports no specific weight-decay outcome in the text; it does not test an efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking below that size.
No comparison of whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
No tests of adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifacts.

rows.subject: FFN
rows.operation_detail: Train on modular addition and measure epoch to 99% test accuracy
rows.measure: Runs reaching 99% test accuracy and median epoch-to-99% among runs that grok
rows.value: 12/20 runs reached 99% within 40k epochs; median 26,300 epochs among runs that grok; 8 remained below 99% at cutoff
rows.uncertainty: Mann-Whitney U =390, p=1.3 × 10−7 (one-sided), treating the 8 censored FFN seeds as tied at 40k
rows.note: The study explicitly calls these runs grokking, but this result does not give the training-accuracy saturation point.
rows.check: For V1 the effect is the delayed jump itself. Grokking appears late (median 26,300 epochs) but only in 12/20 seeds. The other 8 stay below 99% at 40k, so the state is partial on reliability, not because MoE is faster.
